claims.claim: In videotaped nursing home care of people with dementia, resistance to care was more likely to follow elderspeak than ordinary adult talk (about 55 in 100 versus 26 in 100).
claims.supporting_passage: Williams 2009, Abstract: "Videotaped care episodes (n = 80) of nursing home residents with dementia (n = 20) were coded for type of staff communication (normal talk and elderspeak) and subsequent resident behavior (cooperative or resistive to care)." ... "An increased probability of resistiveness to care occurred with elderspeak (.55, 95% CrI, .44-.66), compared with normal talk (.26, 95% CrI, .12-.44)." | Results: "Silence resulted in a probability of .36 for RTC (95% CrI, .21-.55)." | Analyses: "When resident behavior changed, (among states of cooperative, neutral, and RTC), we looked back 7 seconds to determine what staff communication style (normal, elderspeak, or silent) was in use" | Discussion: "A research design that experimentally manipulates nursing staff communication and then assesses resulting resident RTC behaviors is essential to establish a true antecedent-consequent (cause and effect) relationship."
claims.location: Williams 2009: Abstract; Methods (Analyses); Results; Discussion
claims.pico_timeframe: 20 US nursing home residents with dementia, 80 care episodes / exposure: staff elderspeak in the 7 seconds before a change in resident behaviour / comparator: normal adult talk or silence / outcome: probability that the behaviour change was to resistiveness / moment-to-moment, no follow-up
claims.safe_wording: In a US study that filmed 80 care episodes with 20 nursing home residents with dementia, resistance to care followed elderspeak about 55 times in 100, compared with about 26 in 100 after ordinary adult talk. The study shows a link in the moment, not proof that elderspeak causes resistance.
claims.qualifications: Small observational study; probabilities refer to behaviour changes after each type of talk, not to people. Say 'followed' or 'was linked with', never 'caused'. Normal talk was uncommon in the recordings.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The authors state an experiment is needed to establish cause. Some residents were always resistive or always cooperative whatever the talk.

claims.claim: In a small cluster randomised trial in 13 US nursing homes, three one-hour staff sessions (CHAT) reduced staff elderspeak, and residents' resistance to care fell alongside it; the fall in elderspeak held at 3 months, but the fall in resistance at 3 months was not statistically clear.
claims.supporting_passage: Williams 2017, Abstract: "Thirteen NHs were randomized to intervention and control groups. Dyads (n = 42) including 29 staff and 27 persons with dementia were videorecorded during care before and/or after the intervention and at a 3-month follow-up." | Intervention: "The Changing Talk (CHAT) intervention includes three 1-hour sessions that train staff to self-monitor and avoid specific aspects of elderspeak that are associated with RTC." | Results: "On average, the proportion of staff elderspeak use declined from 34.6% of the time (SD = 18.7) prior to the intervention by 13.6% points (SD = 20.00, p = .002) immediately post intervention and 12.2% points (SD = 22.0, p = .016) at 3-month follow-up. Resident RTC was reduced from 35.7% of the time (SD = 23.2) by 15.3% points (SD = 32.4, p = .021) post intervention and 13.4% points (SD = 33.7, p = .077) at 3 months (Table 3)." | Table 3, changes without intervention: staff elderspeak baseline to 1 month mean 1.1 (p = .838); resident RTC baseline to 1 month mean 1.7 (p = .785). | Model for change in RTC: "Explanatory variables in the final model for change in RTC were change in elderspeak (b = 0.43, p < .001) and baseline RTC (b = -0.58, p < .001)." | Discussion: "Only 50% of participating staff attended all sessions despite reminders, a $10 incentive per session, and paid work time for attendance."
claims.location: Williams 2017: Abstract; Intervention section; Results; Table 3; Model for change in RTC; Discussion
claims.pico_timeframe: US nursing home staff and residents with dementia (13 homes; 29 staff, 27 residents in 42 dyads) / three weekly 1-hour CHAT sessions / comparator: periods without intervention (control homes and wait-list before crossover) / outcomes: % of care time with elderspeak and with resident resistiveness on video / immediately after and 3 months after training
claims.safe_wording: In a small trial in 13 US nursing homes, three one-hour training sessions cut the share of care time staff spent in elderspeak from about 35% by about 14 percentage points. Resistance to care fell from about 36% of care time by about 15 points, in step with the fall in elderspeak. Three months later, the drop in elderspeak held (12 points); the drop in resistance (13 points) was no longer statistically clear. Without training, neither changed.
claims.qualifications: Percentages are shares of recorded care time, and the changes are percentage points. Small trial (27 residents), heavy attrition, pooled crossover analysis; only half of staff attended all three sessions. Do not say training 'reduced resistance at 3 months'. Do not claim the effect lasts beyond 3 months.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The intervention predicted the change in elderspeak; the change in resistance was predicted by the change in elderspeak, not directly by group assignment. An online version (CHATO) improved staff knowledge in a pilot trial; its effect on residents was not reported in anything found.

Nearly all (96.6%) of the encounters included some form of elderspeak. Almost half of the care encounters (48.9%) included RoC behaviors. A 10% decrease in elderspeak was associated with a 77% decrease in odds of RoC (OR = 0.23, 95% CI = 0.03, 0.68)" ... "A one-unit decrease in pain severity was associated with 73% reduced odds of RoC"

claims.claim: Elderspeak features include terms of endearment and diminutives ('honey', 'good girl'), 'we' in place of 'you', tag questions, high pitch and exaggerated sing-song intonation.
claims.supporting_passage: Williams 2009, Elderspeak and Dementia Care: "Features of elderspeak include diminutives, inappropriately intimate nominal references, such as “honey” and “good girl.” Collective (plural) pronouns substitute the plural reference when a singular form is grammatically correct and imply that the older adult cannot act independently. For example, “Are we (italics added) ready for our (italics added) bath?” Tag questions prompt resident responses, thus suggesting the resident’s inability to independently choose. “You want to get up now, don’t you (italics added)?”" | Shaw and Gordon 2021, Paralinguistic attributes: "Prosodic characteristics are considered hallmark attributes of elderspeak ... A high-pitched register may be adopted, vocal volume may be inappropriately loud, and speech may be overarticulated. Intonation patterns (i.e., the melody and rhythm) of utterances are often exaggerated." | Semantic attributes: "In observational studies in US nursing homes, diminutives were found in 53% of 80 staff–resident interactions" ... collective pronoun substitution "in 69% of encounters in U.S. nursing homes" | Williams 2017, Behavioral Coding: "Coding of staff elderspeak communication included verbal features (such as diminutives, collective pronoun substitutions) as well as nonverbal prosody (exaggerated voice intonation, high pitch, shouting, exaggerated punctuation)"
claims.location: Williams 2009: Elderspeak and Dementia Care; Shaw and Gordon 2021: Attributes of Elderspeak (Semantic, Paralinguistic); Williams 2017: Behavioral Coding
claims.pico_timeframe: Definitions used in the cited studies; prevalence figures are from US nursing home observations cited in Shaw and Gordon
claims.safe_wording: Elderspeak means talking to an older adult the way people talk to a small child: pet names ('sweetheart', 'good girl'), 'we' instead of 'you' ('Are we ready for our bath?'), questions that answer themselves ('You want to get up now, don't you?'), and a high, sing-song voice.
claims.qualifications: Examples on the visual must be labelled as illustrative phrases. Nursing home frequency figures (53% diminutives, 69% 'we') come from one US study cited in a review; if used, say 'in one US study of 80 nursing home interactions'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Definitions vary between studies; some older definitions also include short sentences and slow speech, which Shaw and Gordon propose to separate out because they can aid comprehension.

numbers.meaning: of 80 US nursing home staff-resident interactions contained diminutives (cited in Shaw and Gordon 2021)
of US nursing home encounters contained collective pronoun substitution (cited in Shaw and Gordon 2021)

claims.claim: Elderspeak is usually meant kindly, but older adults generally find it patronising.
claims.supporting_passage: Lillekroken 2026, Abstract: "Findings suggest that elderspeak is often used with caring intentions and to facilitate care delivery, cooperation and organizational routines. However, these communication practices may simultaneously constrain older adults' autonomy, participation and personhood." | Shaw and Gordon 2021, Abstract: "Elderspeak was generally perceived as patronizing by older adults and speakers were perceived as less respectful." | Contextual and dyadic characteristics: "Despite these positive intentions, cognitively intact older adults usually perceive elderspeak as patronizing" | García 2026, Abstract: "Often rejected as ageist and patronizing, it actually has mixed effects: some features hinder comprehension and well-being, while others aid understanding, social connection, or care."

claims.pico_timeframe: Staff views and older adults' perceptions across qualitative and experimental studies
claims.safe_wording: Staff usually use elderspeak to be kind or to get care done. Older people who are asked mostly find it patronising.
claims.qualifications: Frame as ordinary kindness that misfires, not as staff failing (house rule: never blame whole professions).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: García 2026 argues some features (for example, simpler grammar or warmth) can help; the post should target the pet names, 'we' and sing-song pitch, not all adjustment of speech.

numbers.meaning: qualitative studies in the Lillekroken meta-synthesis

claims.claim: In an experiment with 15 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease, understanding improved when a sentence was repeated, in the same or different words, but not when it was spoken slowly.
claims.supporting_passage: Small 1997, Abstract: "Fifteen patients with mild to moderate AD and 20 healthy older persons were tested on a sentence comprehension task with sentences varying in terms of (a) degree of grammatical complexity, (b) rate of presentation (normal vs. slow), and (c) form of repetition (verbatim vs. paraphrase)." ... "Sentence comprehension improved, however, after the sentence was repeated in either verbatim or parapharsed form. However, the patients' comprehension did not improve for sentences presented at the slow speech rate." ... "The findings challenge the appropriateness of several clinical recommendations."

claims.pico_timeframe: 15 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease (and 20 healthy older controls) / repetition verbatim or paraphrased; slow presentation rate / comparator: single presentation at normal rate / outcome: sentence comprehension on a laboratory task / immediate

claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Shaw and Gordon 2021 report that across studies of older listeners comprehension was generally best with a combination of changes that included slower rate; the evidence on rate alone is mixed. claims.claim: In older adults without dementia, fewer clauses tucked inside sentences and added explanation helped, while short sentences, slow speech and high pitch did not, and led older adults to report more communication problems.
claims.supporting_passage: Kemper and Harden 1999, Abstract: "Providing semantic elaborations and reducing the use of subordinate and embedded clauses benefit older adults and improve their performance on the referential communication task, whereas reducing sentence length, slowing speaking rate, and using high pitch do not. The use of short sentences, a slow rate of speaking, and high pitch resulted in older adults' reporting more communication problems." | Shaw and Gordon 2021, Discussion: "There is evidence that simplification—specifically reducing syntactic and semantic complexity—enhances comprehension but that other modifications (e.g., shortening utterances without reducing complexity) have little or no impact. Perhaps the most important finding is that exaggerated prosody may reduce both actual and perceived comprehension, eradicating the benefits of more helpful attributes like reducing complexity (Kemper & Harden, 1999)."

claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults without dementia / experimentally varied speech features / neutral speech / performance on a referential communication task and self-reported problems / immediate
claims.safe_wording: In experiments with older adults, keeping each sentence to one idea and adding a word of explanation helped. A high, sing-song voice did not help, and made people report more trouble following.
claims.qualifications: Older adults without dementia; laboratory task. Do not present this as a dementia finding.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Shaw and Gordon note studies vary, partly because definitions differ.

claims.claim: What separates plain wording from elderspeak: simplifying grammar, repeating and checking are normal adult speech that can help; elderspeak is marked by childish words (pet names), exaggerated sing-song pitch, and 'we' or tag questions that take the choice away.
claims.supporting_passage: Shaw and Gordon 2021, Operationalizing Elderspeak: "In operationalizing attributes of elderspeak, we propose to remove (or consider separately) attributes that are within the range of normal variation in adult-to-adult speech. Many of these have been repeatedly noted to enhance comprehension, including reduced syntactic complexity, repetitions, verifications, and focal stress. Among the attributes to retain are those that are exaggerated—this is the essence of overaccommodation—and thus give rise to perceptions of patronization." ... "'Elderspeak is a form of communication overaccommodation used with older adults that: is evidenced by inappropriately juvenile lexical choices and/or exaggerated prosody; arises from implicit ageist stereotypes; carries goals of expressing care, exerting control, and/or facilitating comprehension; and may lead to negative self-perceptions in older adults and challenging behaviors in persons with dementia.'" | Pragmatic attributes: "Tag questions, questions attached to the end of a statement providing the illusion of choice" | Williams 2009: collective pronouns "imply that the older adult cannot act independently"
claims.location: Shaw and Gordon 2021: Operationalizing Elderspeak; Pragmatic/discourse attributes; Williams 2009: Elderspeak and Dementia Care
claims.pico_timeframe: Concept analysis across 83 articles, 1981 to 2020
claims.safe_wording: Plain wording is not elderspeak. One idea per sentence, saying it again, and checking you were understood are ordinary adult speech. Elderspeak adds pet names ('love', 'sweetheart'), a high sing-song voice, and 'we' or 'shall we' that make the choice for the person.
claims.qualifications: 'Shall we' is an example of the collective 'we' and softened directive described in these sources; label example phrases as illustrative. This line meets the editor's instruction for C09-19.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: García 2026 argues some elderspeak features may help some people; the core features named here (pet names, exaggerated pitch, 'we') are those linked with patronisation and resistance.

claims.claim: Limitation: the studies are small and old, and across studies a combination of changes that includes a slower rate sometimes helped older listeners, so the finding is that slowing down on its own did not help, not that it harms.
claims.supporting_passage: Shaw and Gordon 2021, Impact of elderspeak on comprehension: "Across studies, comprehension was generally optimized by a combination of decreases in the rate of speech, sentence length, and sentence complexity and increases in the number of words and utterances, redundancy, and semantic content. claims.location: Shaw and Gordon 2021: Abstract; 'Impact of elderspeak on comprehension'
claims.pico_timeframe: Review across studies of older listeners (with and without dementia)
claims.safe_wording: These were small studies (15 people; 18 couples) from the 1990s and 2000s. Slowing down on its own did not help in them; that does not make a calm pace wrong.
claims.qualifications: State sample sizes in the post (judge's request).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Evidence on speech rate is mixed across studies.

claims.claim: Of 67 studies of how doctors communicate with older patients (published since 2000), 16 mentioned hearing loss at all: 6 only mentioned it, 4 used it to exclude people, 2 measured it without further analysis, 3 examined its link with communication, and 1 included an intervention.
claims.supporting_passage: Cohen 2017, Abstract: "We identified 409 papers in the initial search, and included 67 in this systematic review. Of the 67 papers, only 16 studies (23.9%) included any mention of hearing loss. In six of the 16 studies, hearing loss was mentioned only; in four studies, hearing loss was used as an exclusion criterion; and in two studies, the extent of hearing loss was measured and reported for the sample, with no further analysis. Three studies examined or reported on an association between hearing loss and the quality of physician-patient communication. One study included an intervention to temporarily mitigate hearing loss to improve communication."
claims.location: Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Original studies of physician-patient communication with older patients, published from 2000 to about 2016, PubMed only
claims.safe_wording: A review of 67 studies of how doctors talk with older patients, published from 2000 to 2016, found that 16 mentioned hearing loss at all. Four used it to exclude people. Only 3 looked at whether it affected the conversation.
claims.qualifications: Say the date range (judge's request). One database, one search phrase.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Newer studies may do better; not checked.

candidates.reason: All essential claims are supported. Williams 2009 (20 residents, 80 filmed episodes): resistance followed elderspeak 55 in 100 vs 26 in 100 after adult talk; association only. The CHAT cluster randomised trial (13 homes, 27 residents) was read in full: three 1-hour sessions cut elderspeak from 34.6% of care time by 13.6 points, holding at 3 months (12.2 points); resistance fell 15.3 points after training (p = .021) but the 13.4-point fall at 3 months was not statistically clear (p = .077), which answers the judge's question. Resistance change tracked elderspeak change rather than group assignment. Shaw 2022 (88 hospital encounters) found elderspeak in 96.6% and a link with refusal. Definitions and the 'meant kindly' framing are supported by Shaw and Gordon 2021 and a 2026 meta-synthesis. Use only these verified figures, as percentage points of care time, and do not claim the effect on resistance lasted to 3 months. Schedule apart from C09-19 (editor).

Supported from abstracts, with the qualifications the judge asked for. Small 1997 (15 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's): repetition in the same or different words helped comprehension; slow speech did not. Small 2003 (18 couples at home): simple sentences worked, slow speech did not. Kemper and Harden 1999 (older adults without dementia): fewer embedded clauses helped, while short sentences, slow rate and high pitch did not and increased reported problems. Shaw and Gordon 2021 (full text) supplies the editor's required line separating plain wording from elderspeak: grammar simplification, repetition and checking are normal adult speech; elderspeak is marked by juvenile words, exaggerated prosody, 'we' and tag questions. The post must state the sample sizes, say 'slowing down on its own did not help' (not 'slow speech is wrong'), say 'simple' (one idea per sentence), not merely 'short', and reconcile with hearing advice: clear speech helps listeners with hearing loss (Picheny 1985, 5 listeners), and 'clear' is not the same as high-pitched or sing-song. Schedule apart from C09-18.

The essential claim that Talking Mats helps people with dementia feel more involved rests on one small, non-randomised, developer-led study (Murphy and Oliver 2013, 18 couples; abstract only). A 2026 Swedish randomised trial (Bångsbo, 101 home care recipients with dementia, read in full) found no clear difference in involvement or satisfaction between Talking Mats and usual conversations, with high scores in both arms (possible ceiling effect, contamination, staff turnover). A 2023 systematic review found no clear evidence favouring any one tool. The 'Care that works' framing as proposed overstates the evidence. 'Cheap' was not costed; staff needed two days of training and a licence in the trial. 'Developed at the University of Stirling' is supported only by the author affiliation (Talking Mats Centre, University of Stirling Innovation Park).
candidates.revised_angle: Reading the evidence (audience both): a picture-and-mat tool for talking with people with dementia about daily life. In one small study (18 couples) both partners said they felt more involved using it. In a 2026 randomised trial in Swedish home care (101 people), people felt equally involved with or without it, and scores were high in both groups, which leaves little room to show a difference. Takeaway: a structured, visual way to ask the person directly can help some conversations, but the evidence does not show it beats a careful ordinary conversation; ask the person with dementia, not only the family, whatever method is used. Keep neutral about the product (training and licence, no price, no endorsement). If the category needs a 'Care that works' post, use another candidate.

candidates.reason: The empirical core is well supported from full texts: BSL is often a first language and written notes are an unreliable substitute (Rogers 2025 scoping review, 51 studies; Emond 2015; Terry 2024; Selby 2025); Deaf BSL users showed probable underdiagnosis and undertreatment (Emond 2015: high BP readings 37% vs 21%; treated hypertension controlled 42% vs 62%); services often fail to book qualified interpreters and relatives who interpret can leave things out (Rogers 2025; Terry 2024); for older Deaf people patchy interpreter access risks treatment without adequate consent (Lesch 2019). The candidate's legal claim is not verified: the British Sign Language Act 2022 was seen only as a search extract and the 2015 Scottish Act was not checked; per the judge, those Acts do not in any case create a right to an interpreter. The basis for asking is supportable only from secondary sources: the Equality Act duty of reasonable adjustments and, in England only, the Accessible Information Standard (Ahmed 2022, which has an unreadable published correction; Nursing Management 2017). The title has the banned 'X, not Y' shape.
candidates.revised_angle: Who gets left out (audience both): 'For many Deaf people who sign, pen and paper is a second language.' BSL is a language with its own grammar; research with Deaf patients finds written notes and relatives interpreting often leave people without a full picture, and a UK health check found more unrecognised and uncontrolled high blood pressure among Deaf BSL users. Practical close: for any conversation about diagnosis, treatment, consent or discharge, ask the service to book a qualified BSL interpreter; booking is the service's job. Name the Equality Act's reasonable adjustments in general terms and the Accessible Information Standard only as 'in England'. Leave out the BSL Acts unless the statute text is opened and checked. Retitle to avoid the 'interpreter, not a notepad' shape.

candidates.reason: Reserve. The count is supported by the Cohen 2017 systematic review abstract: 16 of 67 studies (published from 2000) mentioned hearing loss, with the breakdown 6/4/2/3/1. The candidate's 'most over 80 have bilateral loss' figure appears only in Cohen's introduction (background), so replace it with the primary US survey figure: 63.1% of adults aged 70 and over had hearing loss; hearing aid use was 40% with moderate loss and 3.4% with mild loss (Lin 2011, 2005 to 2006 data). Add the date range of the review. The bedside habit (check hearing before a decision conversation) is a practice judgement and should be worded as such.
